case.display_title: Diarrhoea, weight loss and a very low blood count

lab_profile.note: The article's own ranges (Table 1), converted to SI.

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on severe anaemia with thrombocytopenia, neutropenia and a haemolytic picture in a 53-year-old woman with ten days of diarrhoea. We reviewed the counts, haemolysis markers and antiglobulin test in the Chart so far. Fragments with a low platelet count must raise a thrombotic microangiopathy, but a high MCV, neutropenia, a reticulocyte count far too low for the degree of anaemia and normal renal function point to a marrow problem with ineffective red cell production. A positive IgG antiglobulin test alone does not establish autoimmune haemolysis. The cause is not yet clear. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Send serum B12 and folate now, before any transfusion
Blood film review and a coagulation screen; calculate the PLASMIC score
Send ADAMTS13 activity if TTP remains a possibility; discuss with us before any plasma exchange
Red cell transfusion only if symptomatic, after the samples are taken; no platelets unless bleeding
Avoid steroids for now

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes a serum B12 of 37 pmol/L. This very low level accounts for the macrocytic pancytopenia and the haemolytic picture with fragments, which result from ineffective red cell production. With a high MCV, normal renal function and no neurological features, the PLASMIC score is low, and we do not recommend plasma exchange. The positive IgG antiglobulin test does not need treatment in its own right. The cause of the low B12 should be established. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now; do not give folic acid on its own
Send intrinsic factor and gastric parietal cell antibodies
Refer to gastroenterology for gastroscopy with gastric body and antral biopsies
Monitor potassium in the first days of replacement
Repeat reticulocytes in 5 to 7 days and the full blood count weekly

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes gastric biopsies showing atrophy of the body and fundic mucosa with intestinal metaplasia. Together with the low B12, this establishes an absorptive cause, and replacement will be lifelong by injection. We expect a reticulocyte response within about a week and a normal count within about two months; iron deficiency may be unmasked as the count recovers. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Lifelong intramuscular hydroxocobalamin: loading doses, then every two to three months
Reticulocytes at day 5 to 7, full blood count and ferritin at 4 to 8 weeks
Check thyroid function periodically
Gastroenterology to advise on endoscopic surveillance of the metaplasia

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on ten days of watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with weight loss and severe anaemia. We reviewed the Chart so far. The diarrhoea is painless and she is haemodynamically stable. An infective cause should be excluded, including Shiga toxin-producing E. coli given the low platelets and fragments. The anaemia with a high MCV raises malabsorption of B12 or folate, from the stomach or the small bowel. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Stool culture, Shiga toxin PCR, C. difficile toxin and ova and parasites
Coeliac serology with total IgA; B12 and folate if not already sent
Oral rehydration and potassium replacement as needed
We will offer gastroscopy with gastric and duodenal biopsies once the counts allow

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise; the Chart now includes a serum B12 of 37 pmol/L. The stomach is the commonest site of B12 malabsorption in an adult with a mixed diet and no bowel surgery; small bowel disease is less likely with normal coeliac serology if sent. The diarrhoea may itself improve with replacement. Happy to review again with the results.
recommendations: Intrinsic factor and gastric parietal cell antibodies
Gastroscopy with biopsies from the gastric body, fundus and antrum, and the duodenum
Serum gastrin and pepsinogen if the antibodies are unhelpful
Start B12 replacement now; it need not wait for endoscopy

consult_notes.note_text: Asked whether this patient has a haemolytic uraemic syndrome. We reviewed the Chart so far. Urine output, creatinine and electrolytes are normal apart from mild potassium and bicarbonate losses from diarrhoea, and there is no proteinuria or haematuria. There is no renal involvement at present, which makes a haemolytic uraemic syndrome unlikely. No indication for dialysis or plasma therapy from our side. Happy to review if the creatinine rises or urine output falls.
recommendations: Urinalysis and daily creatinine while the diagnosis is being established
Oral or intravenous fluids to replace diarrhoeal losses; correct potassium

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to assess for neurological involvement. We examined her: alert and orientated, no focal deficit, normal tone, power and reflexes, intact vibration and joint position sense, negative Romberg test and normal gait. No neurological features of a thrombotic microangiopathy or of a nutritional myelopathy or neuropathy. Happy to review if new symptoms arise.
recommendations: Document the neurological examination as a baseline
Avoid nitrous oxide anaesthesia until the B12 status is known

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to advise on diarrhoea with low counts. We reviewed the Chart so far. She is afebrile with a normal CRP, no travel, no antibiotic exposure and no sick contacts. An infective diarrhoea is possible but does not explain a macrocytic anaemia with neutropenia. Happy to review again with the stool results.
recommendations: Stool culture, Shiga toxin PCR, C. difficile toxin and ova and parasites
HIV test as part of the work-up of pancytopenia
No empirical antibiotics while afebrile and stable

consult_notes.note_text: Asked to review nutrition. About 7 kg weight loss over two to three months with poor appetite; BMI 21. Her usual diet is mixed and adequate in B12 and folate. Intake has fallen recently with the diarrhoea. Happy to review as her appetite recovers.
recommendations: Small frequent meals and oral nutritional supplements while appetite is poor
Weekly weight

Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or Evans syndrome (IgG-positive DAT)
Other causes of pancytopenia: marrow infiltration, aplastic anaemia, HIV

accepted_synonyms: autoimmune atrophic gastritis with vitamin B12 deficiency
secondary_findings: IgG-positive direct antiglobulin test, which the authors discuss as possibly dysimmune; no treatment for autoimmune haemolysis was needed
Prothrombin activity 44%, not explained in the article; modelled as vitamin K deficiency from poor intake and diarrhoea

final_dx.text: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune atrophic gastritis) with severe vitamin B12 deficiency, presenting as pancytopenia with haemolysis and schistocytes that mimicked a thrombotic microangiopathy (pseudo-TMA)

key_discriminators: inappropriately low reticulocytes (92 x10^9/L) despite haemolysis and Hb 51 g/L
normal renal function and no neurological impairment
PLASMIC score 4 (low risk of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency)
fundic atrophy with intestinal metaplasia on gastric biopsy

must_do.text: Measure vitamin B12 and folate in macrocytic pancytopenia, ideally before any transfusion
Weigh the risk of TTP before any plasma exchange: blood film with fragments, coagulation and renal function (PLASMIC score); ADAMTS13 if TTP remains possible
Measure the reticulocyte count and recognise that a low count with haemolysis points to ineffective erythropoiesis
Find the cause: intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies, and gastroscopy with gastric biopsies
Plan to confirm the response: reticulocytes within about a week, then the blood count

must_not_do.text: Start plasma exchange for presumed TTP without weighing B12 deficiency and the PLASMIC score
Treat as autoimmune haemolytic anaemia with steroids or rituximab on the IgG DAT alone
Give folic acid without B12 replacement
Transfuse platelets when there is no bleeding and a thrombotic microangiopathy is still possible

ground_truth.outcome: Rapid improvement: diarrhoea resolved by day 4 and a reticulocyte response by day 7 of replacement, without other treatment. Follow-up values not reported.

rubric.text: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune gastritis) causing severe B12 deficiency with a pseudo-microangiopathic picture
Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia, cause not established
Megaloblastic anaemia without naming B12, or folate deficiency
TTP, HUS, another microangiopathy, warm AIHA or myelodysplasia as the final diagnosis
Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: Severe B12 deficiency can mimic a thrombotic microangiopathy: schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, very high LDH and low haptoglobin.
A low reticulocyte count with haemolysis means ineffective erythropoiesis, not peripheral destruction alone; with a high MCV and neutropenia it points to the marrow.
The PLASMIC score (platelets, haemolysis, no cancer or transplant, MCV, INR, creatinine) helps decide against plasma exchange; a high MCV lowers the score.
Take B12 and folate samples before transfusion, and never give folic acid alone to a patient who may be B12 deficient.
A positive IgG DAT is not proof of autoimmune haemolysis; weigh it against the whole picture before steroids.
ground_truth.treatment_given: Vitamin B12 replacement (route, dose and schedule not reported). No plasma exchange.

reports.impression: Macrocytic red cells with fragments, hypersegmented neutrophils and thrombocytopenia.
reports.report_text: Red cells show marked anisopoikilocytosis with many oval macrocytes. Red cell fragments (schistocytes) are present, about 2% of red cells. Occasional nucleated red cells. Polychromasia is scanty. Neutrophils are reduced, and several are hypersegmented (six or more lobes). Platelets are reduced, with no clumps.

reports.impression: Macrocytic anaemia with fragments and hypersegmented neutrophils; poor reticulocyte response.
reports.report_text: Film reviewed by a haematopathologist. Red cells show marked anisopoikilocytosis with many oval macrocytes. Red cell fragments (schistocytes) are present, about 2% of red cells. Occasional nucleated red cells. Polychromasia is scanty. Neutrophils are reduced, and several are hypersegmented (six or more lobes). Platelets are reduced, with no clumps. No spherocytes, blasts or parasites seen. Comment: the reticulocyte response is inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia; suggest serum B12 and folate before transfusion, and ADAMTS13 if a thrombotic microangiopathy is still being considered.

reports.impression: Hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and megaloblastic change.
reports.report_text: Particulate, markedly hypercellular aspirate. Erythroid hyperplasia with megaloblastic erythropoiesis: large erythroblasts with fine, open chromatin, prominent nucleoli and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony. Giant metamyelocytes and band forms are present. Megakaryocytes are present in normal numbers. Blasts 1%. No abnormal infiltrate. See the iron stain report.

reports.impression: Markedly hypercellular marrow with erythroid expansion and megaloblastic change.
reports.report_text: Trephine core with marked hypercellularity (about 90%). Expanded erythroid precursors, including megaloblasts with fine chromatin and prominent nucleoli. Granulopoiesis is present with left-shifted maturation; megakaryocytes are adequate. No fibrosis on reticulin stain. No infiltrate or granulomas.

reports.impression: Increased storage iron; no ring sideroblasts.
reports.report_text: Perls stain shows increased storage iron (grade 3) in marrow fragments. No ring sideroblasts are seen.

reports.impression: No evidence of a clonal haematological neoplasm.
reports.report_text: Erythroid precursors are increased. Myeloid and monocytic maturation patterns are normal. CD34-positive blasts under 1% with a normal phenotype. B cells polyclonal; no abnormal population.
Twenty metaphases analysed at a 400-band level. 46,XX. No clonal abnormality detected.
Two hundred interphase nuclei scored per probe. Normal signal patterns for 5q31, 7q31, chromosome 8 centromere and 20q12; no deletion or gain detected.

reports.impression: Pale, thin mucosa of the gastric body and fundus; antrum and duodenum normal. Biopsies taken.
reports.report_text: Endoscopy to the second part of the duodenum. Normal oesophagus. The mucosa of the gastric body and fundus is pale and thin, with prominent submucosal vessels and loss of rugal folds; the antrum looks normal. No ulcer or mass. Normal duodenum. Biopsies taken from the body, fundus and antrum for histology.

reports.impression: Atrophy of the body and fundic mucosa with intestinal metaplasia; antrum spared; no dysplasia.
reports.report_text: Biopsies from the gastric body and fundus: atrophy of the oxyntic (fundic) mucosa with loss of parietal and chief cells and a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the lamina propria. Intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells. No dysplasia. Antral biopsy: mild chronic inflammation without atrophy. No Helicobacter-like organisms seen.

The liver is normal in size and echotexture with no focal lesion. The gallbladder is thin-walled without calculi, and the common bile duct is not dilated. The spleen measures 10.5 cm. Both kidneys are normal in size and echotexture without hydronephrosis. No free fluid or mass.

Complete colonoscopy to the caecum with intubation of the terminal ileum; fair bowel preparation. Normal colonic and ileal mucosa. No polyps, ulceration or bleeding source. Random colonic biopsies taken: normal colonic mucosa, no microscopic colitis.
